title: Mashed Potato from Fresh, Made with Milk

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potato made from fresh potatoes and milk is a smooth, creamy side dish. The potatoes are boiled until tender, then mashed and blended with milk, butter, and optionally seasoned with salt and pepper.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes are one of the most widely consumed root vegetables worldwide.
Traditional mash is often made from yellow or white potatoes, which have a lower starch content than red varieties.
Adding milk creates a lighter texture and a subtle dairy flavor.
In many cuisines, cream, butter, or cheese are added for extra richness.
Mashed potatoes serve as a base for casseroles and dishes like shepherd's pie.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium, which helps maintain normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C source
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain vitamin C, supporting immune health and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates for energy
items.content: The starch in potatoes offers a steady release of energy.

items.title: Betaine content
items.content: Betaine in potatoes supports liver function and homocysteine metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from milk
items.content: Milk adds calcium and, when fortified, vitamin D, which are important for bone health.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk allergy may experience reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, so portion control is advised for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Excessive salt added during preparation can increase sodium intake, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: If cooked potatoes are left at room temperature too long, bacteria may grow and cause foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the mash hot as a side to meat, fish, or vegetable dishes. Top with fried onions, fresh herbs, grated cheese, or garlic for extra flavor. For a lighter version, use low‑fat milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftover mash in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat with a splash of milk or cream to restore creaminess. It can be frozen for up to 2 months, though texture may become slightly watery after thawing.
